sentences.text: Rhynchaeites is an extinct genus of wading birds whose name translates to "beak fossil" in Greek.
This ancient bird possessed much shorter legs than its modern relatives and lacked sensory nerves in its bill.
The type species Rhynchaeites messelensis is known from many well-preserved fossils found in the Lutetian-aged Messel pit in Germany.
A third species, Rhynchaeites mcfaddeni, was described in 2026 based on a largely complete specimen from the Green River Formation in the United States.
Rhynchaeites is one of the oldest known members of the ibis family.
The genus was identified as an early ibis in 1983, after previously being thought to be related to painted-snipes or other charadriiforms.
A second species, Rhynchaeites litoralis, was described in 2023 from the Ypresian-aged London Clay of England.
Potential leg bone fossils of Rhynchaeites have been found in the earliest Ypresian Fur Formation in Denmark.
Rhynchaeites species inhabited different environments, with R. messelensis living in freshwater and R. litoralis in coastal areas.
Because the bill lacked touch receptors, the animal likely relied on sight to find food rather than the tactile probing used by modern ibises.
Rhynchaeites is classified as a stem-group member of the Threskiornithidae family.
Rhynchaeites lived in Europe and North America during the Eocene epoch.
The genus lived between 56 and 41.03 million years ago during the Ypresian to Lutetian stages.
Researchers hypothesize that the parrot-like fossil Mopsitta tanta might actually be a leg bone belonging to Rhynchaeites.
